content: An aqueous solution is a type of solution where water acts as the solvent. In chemical equations, this is typically denoted with the subscript (aq). The term aqueous refers to substances that are related to, similar to, or dissolved in water. Water is an exceptional solvent due to its chemical properties and natural abundance, making it a widely used solvent in chemistry. Substances that do not dissolve well in water are termed hydrophobic, meaning water-fearing, while those that dissolve readily are called hydrophilic, meaning water-loving. A common example of a hydrophilic substance is sodium chloride, or table salt. Acids and bases, as defined by the Arrhenius theory, are also examples of aqueous solutions. The solubility of a substance in water depends on its ability to overcome the strong intermolecular forces between water molecules. If a substance cannot dissolve in water, it will form a precipitate. Aqueous solutions that conduct electricity efficiently contain strong electrolytes, which are substances that completely ionize in water. In contrast, solutions with weak electrolytes conduct electricity poorly because they only partially ionize. Non-electrolytes are substances that dissolve in water but do not produce ions. When performing calculations involving reactions between aqueous solutions, it is essential to know the concentration or molarity of the solutions. The concentration is typically expressed in terms of the solute's form before it dissolves. Regarding aqueous solubility, the following general rules apply: All compounds containing sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), and ammonium (NH₄⁺) ions are soluble in water. All nitrates (NO₃⁻) and acetates (CH₃COO⁻) are soluble in water. Most chlorides (Cl⁻) and sulfates (SO₄²⁻) are soluble in water, with exceptions such as silver chloride (AgCl), lead(II) chloride (PbCl₂), mercury(I) chloride (Hg₂Cl₂), barium sulfate (BaSO₄), and lead(II) sulfate (PbSO₄). Most carbonates (CO₃²⁻), phosphates (PO₄³⁻), sulfides (S²⁻), and hydroxides (OH⁻) are insoluble in water, except for compounds like lithium hydroxide (LiOH), sodium hydroxide (NaOH), potassium hydroxide (KOH), and aqueous ammonia (NH₃(aq)).
